power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Calibrated trust is considered an important factor for human-system interaction in decision-making.
However, definitions of calibrated trust are heterogeneous and research often lacks conceptual clarity.
In our work, we conducted a theoretical integration to summarize approaches defining and operationalizing calibrated trust in automation and AI.

We then mapped these approaches onto the trust development process that builds on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995).

text.text: The resulting Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) offers theoretical clarity and actionable insights for improving trust calibration by identifying six calibration points that can be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and, as a consequence, effective human oversight: maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation.
The TCa-P emphasizes that trust calibration is not monolithic but instead happens at different points along the trust development process.

text.text: While most prior work shares the goal of optimizing joint human-system performance, it often remains unclear which aspects of the human-system interaction should be calibrated, and how.

This leaves research and practice with uncertainty in communication about trust calibration and, more importantly, in identifying design and intervention opportunities to achieve calibrated trust and appropriate trusting behavior.

To address these limitations, we analyzed prior research to identify the diversity in what has been called "calibrated trust" (including related terms like "appropriate", "adequate", and "warranted" trust).
We then mapped the emerging concepts throughout the trust development process (Mayer et al., 1995; Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025).

text.text: As a result of our analysis, we advocate for a more holistic process-based perspective on trust calibration, and thereby contrast prior monolithic perspectives on trust calibration.

We offer an integrative solution by providing six calibration points within the Trust Calibration-Points Framework (TCa-P), which allow to specify which aspects need to be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and allow for a targeted discussion on how they could be calibrated.
Our analysis of trust literature builds on the propositions of the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (TrAM; Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995).

text.text: Based on this elaboration, we argue that the diverse conceptualizations of calibrated trust and related terms (e.g., warranted trust, justified trust, and appropriate reliance) address important single aspects of "trust calibration" along the trust development process, which are all required to optimize joint human-system performance.
From there, we argue for a comprehensive, integrative mapping and a holistic perspective on trust calibration, which we then outline in our proposed Trust Calibration-Points Framework.

text.text: The allocation of concepts reflects our interpretation of the literature and is intended as a conceptual rather than a definitive classification.
Because trust calibration terminology varies considerably across disciplines, individual authors might classify their concepts differently.

text.text: In this sense, perfect calibration is achieved when users rely on correct system outputs and override incorrect ones, while miscalibration occurs when users over-rely on inaccurate outputs or under-rely on correct ones.

Typically, this form of calibration is measured by factors such as decision accuracy (e.g., Schoeffer et al., 2025; Vereschak et al., 2021), and is operationalized by comparing the joint decision accuracy against two benchmarks: Human performance alone and the system performance alone (e.g., Rieger & Manzey, 2022).

text.text: These approaches evaluate trust calibration post-hoc, after outcomes are known, providing an external diagnostic perspective on the human-system interaction.
A challenge arising from this approach is that it neither provides insights into the factors leading to suboptimal performance nor ways to achieve better calibration.
For example, it is unclear whether the suboptimal performance was due to an inaccurate trustworthiness assessment or due to an inaccurate risk assessment.

Consequently, calibrated trust in this sense only captures the outcome of the trust development process and thus offers a symptomatic description rather than an identification of root causes or a solution for (mis)calibration.

Calibrated trust has been conceptualized as an accurate trustworthiness assessment (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025), i.e., the match between system characteristics and perceived trustworthiness (de Visser et al., 2016; Wischnewski et al., 2023).

In other words, if the trustworthiness assessment is adequate given the cues available to the trustor, the trustworthiness assessment can be considered justified, even if it turns out to be incorrect (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) leading, for instance, to negative joint performance consequences.

text.text: While it is important to distinguish that an assessment of trustworthiness can be justified but inaccurate, this understanding of calibrated trust again focuses only on a single aspect of the trust development process, neglecting that even a perfectly justified trustworthiness assessment can be inaccurate, and hence may not necessarily lead to optimal joint performance.

text.text: It seems that this cross-use bears potential for future confusion, which we want to prevent at this point.
In the trust development process, alignment happens as a part of the trustworthiness assessment.
More specifically, therein alignment mainly refers to the degree of overlap between the individual standards of the trustee and the trustor.

The previous section pointed out problems with existing conceptualizations of "calibrated trust", which are fragmented and often narrowly focused on isolated stages of the trust development process (cf.
Figure 1, Table 1).

text.text: While each perspective sheds light on important facets of human-system interaction, none sufficiently captures the complexity required to systematically diagnose or improve joint human-system performance.
These partial views limit both theoretical clarity and practical applicability.

Notably, what unites all research on calibrated trust is its shared goal: optimizing joint human-system performance, as well as minimizing harmful errors and problematic outcomes (e.g. unfair discrimination) that might be introduced by implementing automated systems into high-risk contexts.

We share this goal, and introduce the Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) that enables researchers to investigate and understand why the joint human-system performance in each context is suboptimal, and how it could be optimized.
The TCa-P aims to unify the different conceptualizations of trust calibration along the trust development process, thereby offering a structured basis for diagnosis, measurement, and intervention.

With the TCa-P we propose six calibration points that aim at differentiating and diagnosing the single parts within the trust development process that might hinder optimal joint performance of humans and systems.
We consider these calibration points the levers and knobs to tune to calibrate joint human-system performance.
It is important to note that we assume a context where the preconditions for trust being relevant are met (Mayer et al., 1995).
text.formatted: It is important to note that we assume a context where the preconditions for trust being relevant are met <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Mayer et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: That means, a) humans need to have the freedom to decide (not) to trust a system (e.g., if the human fears to face punishment when rejecting system advice, following system advice may not reflect trust), and b) humans need to be in appropriate contexts to make this decision (e.g., avoiding excessive time or peer pressure which may render any decision than to follow and use a system impossible), and c) the outcome of trusting or relying on a system needs to be uncertain to a degree (e.g., trust is not an issue if the human knows a system is always right, like a calculator), and d) there needs to be something at stake for the human that provides a perceived benefit of trusting (e.g., higher efficiency), but at the same time puts them at risk, and renders them vulnerable to the outcome of the system's advice or action (e.g., the human is responsible for the outcome).
All these factors are prerequisites to talk about trust and thus also for trust calibration.
If external factors are determining behavior, trust calibration may not be the primary concern.

text.text: The Trust-Calibration-Points Framework Note.
Shows the six calibration points (blue circles) within the trust development process (see Figure 1).
Definition: The degree to which the set expectations of a system match the achievable joint performance of a human-system team, i.e. their joint potential.
Miscalibration: Occurs when expectations exceed or fall short of the team's actual performance potential.
Implication: Interventions may target the wrong calibration point instead of improving the team's actual capabilities.
To counteract miscalibration, it is important to understand the individual contributions and limitations of the humansystem team to calibrate performance expectations.
An AI triage system identifies urgent cases with 85% accuracy.
Responder A is 70% accurate and their errors mainly overlap with those of the system, so the team cannot be expected to exceed 85%.

Responder B is 90% accurate and holds distinct experience with warm-climate casualties that the system lacks; here joint performance could in principle reach 95%, but only if the two sets of capabilities are successfully aggregated.
Definition: The degree to which the perceived trustworthiness matches the actual trustworthiness (accuracy) and the degree to which a trustor correctly uses available cues (justification).

Miscalibration: Occurs when an assessment is inaccurate, i.e., the trustor's perceived trustworthiness does not match the system's actual trustworthiness, or unjustified, i.e., the trustor does not utilize all available cues correctly.
Implication: The cause for miscalibration needs to be specified, and targeted interventions on the system and trustor side need to be derived.
Responder C follows an incorrect recommendation and moves on from a seriously injured.
In their experience, the system had never erred; its reported accuracy of 85% exceeded their own 70%.
A sudden system malfunction was caused by overheating, but no cue signaled that malfunction.
The responder's trustworthiness assessment was justified but resulted in an undesired outcome, which points to a system-side problem: relevant cues indicating system error were unavailable.
A possible solution is to make cues available that indicate when a system recommendation should be verified.
Definition: The degree to which the individual standards of at least two parties (e.g., system and user) overlap.

Miscalibration: Occurs when standards are misaligned, and especially when parties are unaware of their misalignment resulting in incorrect assumptions of the system's capabilities and values, and consequently unwanted outcomes.
Implication: System standards need to be transparent, and the standards of different parties assessing system trustworthiness need to be explicit.
Two responders rely on the same triage tool, but have different individual standards.
Responder D wants to maximize the number of survivors, while responder E aims to treat all critically injured first, even if they may have a low chance of survival.
The system is aligned with responder E and prioritizes the most critical first.
Responder D might feel uneasy with the system's recommendations and reject using it or might not notice the misalignment and turn out unsatisfied with the result.
Definition: The degree to which a trustors' perceived risks and benefits match the actual risks and benefits associated with the use of a system in a given situation.
Miscalibration: Occurs when the stakes of a situation are over or underestimated.
Inaccurate risk-benefit assessments can lead to insufficient monitoring and trustworthiness assessment, or to rejection of useful system outcomes.
Implication: Systems and providers should clearly communicate the risks and benefits associated with system use in context.
Commander F, responsible for the operation, is among the injured, but not prioritized by the system.
After the examination, responder G receives following evaluation: "Medical shock."
Responder H sees the extended statement "Medical shock and heat exhaustion."
Although statistically less probable, Responder H perceives it as more urgent and thus more likely, overestimates the risk of inaction, and overrides the decision without checking.
Adding context (e.g., "of 100 critical cases, only 10 have both") could have prevented this fallacy and fostered a better-calibrated riskbenefit assessment.
CP 5: Dispositions Definition: The degree to which extreme dispositions, attitudes, stable dispositions and biases deteriorate trust-related assessments or directly guide behavior.
Miscalibration: Occurs when users are biased due to extreme attitudes.
Implication: Training and experience can help to reduce unwanted biases.
Responders I and J are told the system is 85% accurate.

Responder I, generally expects AI systems to generally be reliable, starts using the system without hesitation, and requires little evidence before accepting recommendation, possibly overlooking an error.
Responder J approaches technology with skepticism; he requires extensive verification even in situations where verification provides little benefit.
Their commander must anticipate their individual dispositions and train them accordingly to avoid miscalibration.
Definition: The degree to which observable trusting behavior (e.g. monitoring behavior, reliance on system advice) follow a predefined ideal behavior.
Miscalibration: Occurs when behavior deviates from ideal behavior, which is e.g. reflected in insufficient monitoring or extensive control.
Implication: Checklists and training can help attaining to an ideal behavior, but this must not necessarily result in perfect outcomes.
The response protocol defines the ideal behavior as verifying every recommendation below a confidence threshold of 80%.
The system now provides an accurate recommendation with 75% confidence.
Responder K verifies the recommendation, while responder J relies on it without additional verification.
Although both responders achieve accurate results, only responder L is behaviorally calibrated.
The example in this table describes a mass-casualty incident.
A mass-casualty incident produces more casualties than the available 327 responders can treat simultaneously, so treatment must be prioritized.

In our example, responders are working in field operations under unusually 328 high temperatures and are equipped with an AI triage decision-support system that examines a casualty and recommends a priority level; the 329 responder may follow or override the recommendation.
Calibration Point 1 requires setting realistic expectations regarding the outcome, i.e. the joint performance potential of human-system teams.
Without setting realistic expectations it is unclear whether the observed joint human-system performance reflects the best possible, or at least an acceptable joint outcome.

Often, when introducing an AI system, it is implicitly assumed that human-system collaboration will result in synergy, where the joint performance exceeds the individual performances of both partners, or at least, augmentation, where the joint performance exceeds one partner's individual capacity.
Whereas synergy is rare, augmentation is more commonly observed (Vaccaro et al., 2024).

text.text: In other words, human-AI teams often tend to perform worse than either the human or AI working alone (but see Cabrera et al., 2023; de Visser & Parasuraman, 2011; Roemer et al., 2026; Wickens & Dixon, 2007).

text.text: Maximum joint performance represents the theoretical best performance given the individual contributions of the team members; it does not necessarily equal perfect performance, which is the flawless completion of a task.
Instead, maximum joint performance provides a reasonable benchmark on what can be expected from human-system collaboration.

Maximum joint performance depends on complementarity, i.e., the diversity of unique performance contributions of humans and systems (Burton et al., 2024; de Winter & Dodou, 2014; Metcalfe et al., 2021).

text.text: For this calibration point, miscalibrations means that expectations about the joint performance of human-system teams exceed or fall short of their joint potential.
This might lead to wrongful claims that problems in human-system interaction occurred at other points within the trust development process (Calibration Points 2-6).

For example, if a pilot's skills declined after relying on the autopilot for substantial time, their manual skills may no longer enable them to intervene effectively, even if they notice system malfunction and are fully aware of the risks.
In this case, the implicitly expected joint human-system performance exceeds their joint potential.

Given the human should remain part of the dyad, addressing this miscalibration requires acknowledging the reduced human contribution and providing appropriate training, rather than attempting to improve risk communication or the presentation of system failures.
The key takeaway is that expectations should match the human-AI teams potential based on their capabilities.
Neither users nor AI systems can magically increase their own capabilities, and hence their contribution to the joint task, when teaming up.
Synergy is only possible if the individual contributions of humans and AI are diverse, complementary and allow for efficient aggregation (Burton et al., 2024).

Calibration Point 2 refers to the accuracy of the trustworthiness assessment, i.e. whether the trustor's perceived trustworthiness matches the system's actual trustworthiness (cf.
TrAM, Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025, as well as section Theoretical Background and Figure 4 below).

text.text: The accuracy of the trustworthiness assessment depends on the availability and relevance of cues on the side of the system, and on the detection and correct utilization of cues on the side of the trustor.
Only if relevant cues are available to the trustor, and only if trustors detect those cues and interpret them correctly an accurate trustworthiness assessment is possible.

If a trustor utilizes all available cues correctly but there are not enough relevant cues (e.g., due to the system's opaqueness Barredo Arrieta et al., 2020), the trustor's assessment is justified but inaccurate (Funder, 1995).

Justified Trustworthiness Assessment
Note.
The depicted model is based on the considerations of the TrAM (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The depicted model is based on the considerations of the TrAM <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">(Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therein, a trustworthiness assessment is accurate when the actual trustworthiness of a system matches the perceived trustworthiness of the trustor (upper purple connection line).

A trustworthiness assessment is justified (lower blue connection line), when available cues are detected and correctly utilized by the trustor, independent of the accuracy of the trustworthiness assessment.
The differentiation between an accurate and a justified trustworthiness assessment helps to understand the causes of inaccurate assessments.
An inaccurate, but justified assessment shows that relevant system cues are missing which emphasizes necessary changes on the system side.
An inaccurate and unjustified assessment shows that trustors cannot detect or correctly utilize the available cues, an issue with the interface or human operator.
An accurate, but unjustified assessment might be the result of lucky guessing, and may lead to "learned carelessness" (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) posing a risk of future errors.
text.formatted: An accurate, but unjustified assessment might be the result of lucky guessing, and may lead to "learned carelessness" <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">(Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010)</ref> posing a risk of future errors.

text.text: As such, the goal should be to have trustors being able to build justified and accurate assessments.
Inaccurate trustworthiness assessment of the system can lead to tragic consequences, as illustrated by the USS Vincennes incident in 1988 (Rochlin, 1990).
text.formatted: Inaccurate trustworthiness assessment of the system can lead to tragic consequences, as illustrated by the USS Vincennes incident in 1988 <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">(Rochlin, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Operators of the ship's anti-aircraft system misidentified a commercial aircraft as an attacking military aircraft, and shot it down, because the system provided misleading and poorly designed cues.
The operators of the system relied on the available, and seemingly consistent cues, making their assessment to shoot down the aircraft justified from their perspective, while ultimately inaccurate.
The result was the downing of the Iranian Flight 655 and the loss of 290 civilian lives.
Key to achieving accurate and justified trustworthiness assessments is the relevance, availability, detection, and utilization of cues to assess the trustworthiness of a system.
Depending on why a trustworthiness assessment is inaccurate different steps need to be taken to improve its accuracy.
If a trustor's assessment is justified but inaccurate, the system needs to be adapted or redesigned, in a way that makes relevant cues available.

This could happen by realizing AI systems with metacognitive capabilities (S. G. B. text.text: Calibration Point 3 is closely related to the field of value alignment (Bhat et al., 2024; Gabriel, 2020; Pflanzer et al., 2023), which addresses the challenge that AI systems should align with the individual standards of different trustors, while at the same time they need to align with broader ethical principles and legal requirements (Figure 5).

text.text: We here define alignment as the degree to which the individual standards of at least two parties overlap.

Building on the TrAM (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025), individual standards reflect the values, norms, moral beliefs, preferences, decision-making styles, and goals that determine what each party considers to be a trustworthy AI system.

text.text: These standards may differ across parties due to pluralistic moral beliefs (Gabriel, 2020; Hu et al., 2025), varying cultural backgrounds (Awad et al., 2018), motivations (Durán & Jongsma, 2021), and goals (Gabriel & Keeling, 2025).

text.text: Parties can be trustors (e.g., end-users, or developers; Saffarizadeh et al., 2024), trustees (e.g., an AI system), and third parties (e.g., observing researchers with specific normative standards, more abstract human values or ethics, Gabriel, 2020; or agreed upon standards, Jobin et al., 2019).

text.text: To clarify, Calibration Point 2 concerns whether trustors accurately assess a system's individual standards, Calibration Point 3 concerns whether the standards of a trustor and a system align.
Consequently, alignment and accurate trustworthiness assessments are conceptually independent.
Multiple parties may be aligned without being aware of it, or fully aware of their misalignment.

text.text: To illustrate, consider a setting with three parties: An AI system (the trustee), a user of the AI system (the trustor), and a third party who evaluates the joint performance of the human-AI team according to ethical standards (Figure 5).

text.text: This triadic relationship entails three alignment relationships.

First, alignment between trustee and trustor means that the AI system aligns with the user's individual standards and thereby foster trust and acceptance (Hu et al., 2025; J. McVay et al., 2025; Rauch et al., 2025; Shortland et al., 2025; Summerville et al., 2025).

text.text: Second, alignment between trustee and third party concerns whether the AI system adheres to broader ethical, safety, or regulatory standards that aim to ensure societal benefit (for an overview see Jobin et al., 2019), which may conflict with individual user preferences (i.e., third parties; Gabriel & Keeling, 2025).

text.text: For instance, such conflicts may arise when personal convenience leads to environmental harm, or when speed undermines safety (Phillips & Malle, 2025).

text.text: Third, alignment between trustor and third party reflects whether trustors share broader normative principles of third parties.
Problems could arise when parties are misaligned or when they are not aware of their (mis)alignment.

Misalignment may especially occur in cases of normative uncertainty, for example when different ethical principles could legitimately guide a system's behavior (e.g., maximizing life expectancy vs. minimizing suffering, Durán & Jongsma, 2021).

text.text: In such cases of moral uncertainty, it is key that all parties are aware of their degree of alignment, which is reflected in pluralistic alignment approaches (Hu et al., 2024 (Hu et al., , 2025;; Lyons et al., 2023; Pflanzer et al., 2023; Schelble et al., 2026; Sorensen et al., 2024).

text.text: Unawareness might be especially problematic when people accept a system, but with wrong expectations about its intended purpose or optimization goals (Durán & Jongsma, 2021).

text.text: Unawareness of misalignment could be enhanced through the false-consensus effect (i.e. one party assumes that their individual standards and those of another party are aligned, Ross et al., 1977), through automation bias and complacency (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010).

text.text: Those may lead people to assume that an automated system works perfectly.
A further unawareness of misalignment may arise when people use AI agents to act on their behalf.

Previous work has highlighted that acting through AI agents to direct other humans can enable unethical behavior (Gratch & Fast, 2022), or improve cooperation (de Melo et al., 2019) depending on how users can program their agent.

text.text: It is important to recognize that trustworthiness assessment (Calibration Point 2) and alignment of standards (Calibration Point 3) require different diagnoses and therefore different interventions.
More specifically, when third parties (e.g., researchers) assess the accuracy of a trustor's trustworthiness assessment they need to be aware of the trustor's individual standards.
Otherwise, third parties could confuse inaccurate trustworthiness assessment with misalignments, thereby overlooking the actual cause and hindering the application of effective countermeasures.

Whereas inaccuracies in trustworthiness assessment may be addressed by improving relevant system cues or by user training, misalignment requires adapting either the trustor's or the system's standards, or deciding not to use the system.

To address misalignment, the standards of a system could be aligned with those of a trustor either during the design of the system or they could also be adapted automatically during interaction with the system (de Visser et al., 2023; Jelínek et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To address misalignment, the standards of a system could be aligned with those of a trustor either during the design of the system or they could also be adapted automatically during interaction with the system <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(de Visser et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Jelínek et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, alignment is not always appropriate, e.g., if the trustor's individual standards conflict with ethical or legal standards.
In these cases, interventions could focus on changing trustors' individual standards.

In cases of moral uncertainty (Baum & Slavkovik, 2025) or in cases in which multiple legitimate options exist (Deutsch, 1975; Summerville et al., 2025), it may be neither possible nor appropriate to change the trustor's standards, but instead to change the system's standards to match those of the individual trustor (J. McVay et al., 2025; Summerville et al., 2025).

text.text: In these cases, it is important that individual standards are made transparent, enabling accurate trustworthiness assessments (J. Y. C. Chen et al., 2018; Endsley, 2023).

text.text: Calibration Point 4 refers to the accuracy of the risk-benefit assessment.
Risk refers to the likelihood and severity of potential losses, such as the probability and cost of an error (e.g., an accident).
Benefits refer to the anticipated gains (e.g., productivity, increased performance).
These considerations include what is at stake, how large the anticipated benefit is, and what the consequences of failure would be.
The fact that Mayer et al. (1995) used the term perceived risk highlights that there might be deviances from actual risk associated with a given behavior.
text.formatted: The fact that <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Mayer et al. (1995)</ref> used the term perceived risk highlights that there might be deviances from actual risk associated with a given behavior.

text.text: This is also highlighted by Slovic (1987) who referred to intuitive risk judgments of lay people (or the public) as risk perceptions.
text.formatted: This is also highlighted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b187">Slovic (1987)</ref> who referred to intuitive risk judgments of lay people (or the public) as risk perceptions.

text.text: He outlines how risk perceptions differ between experts and lay people, and between people with different backgrounds.

Moreover, he depicts that different criteria might be applied when risk is assessed by experts (e.g., annual mortality rates) and lay people (e.g., uncertainty surrounding a risk, and a potential influence on future generations).

Risk-benefit assessments influence the trust development process (Chancey et al., 2017; Lyons & Stokes, 2012) and have been discussed under situational risk (Hoff & Bashir, 2015) and situation-specific trust (Cohen et al., 1997) in the context of automation. Satterfield et al. (2017), for example, support this assumption by showing that in high-risk situations compared to low-risk situations, participants were more likely to intervene manually in a task that was delegated to an automated agent.

text.text: Participants were thus less likely to show trusting behavior in high-risk situations, although they perceived the automation equally trustworthy respectively trusted the agent similarly in the high-and low-risk conditions.
There is further evidence that this relationship inverts with simpler automation (Fahnenstich et al., 2024).

text.text: Following from that, if trustors inaccurately assess risks and benefits this may lead to inadequate behavior and potentially also influence the depth of the trustworthiness assessment (Schlicker, Lechner, et al., 2025).

text.text: Inaccuracies of the risk-benefit assessment can arise out of limited available, relevant information, and due to limited detection and incorrect interpretation of available information, and individual circumstances.
In risk-benefit assessments, often only partial information is available on the exact probabilities of both positive and negative outcomes of a decision.

Additionally, detection may be limited by people's tendency to search for satisfactory rather than optimal decisions, as outlined in the concept of "bounded rationality" (Gigerenzer & Goldstein, 1996; Gigerenzer & Selten, 2002; Simon, 1990).

text.text: With respect to the interpretation of available information, research on cognitive heuristics shows that people are generally poor at assessing risks, even when probabilities are explicit.
For instance, the conjunction fallacy illustrates how individuals may judge a combination of characteristics as more likely than a single characteristic (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983).
text.formatted: For instance, the conjunction fallacy illustrates how individuals may judge a combination of characteristics as more likely than a single characteristic <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">(Tversky & Kahneman, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, "loss aversion" refers to the tendency that people react more sensitive to estimated losses than to equivalent gains (Kahneman et al., 1991).
text.formatted: Similarly, "loss aversion" refers to the tendency that people react more sensitive to estimated losses than to equivalent gains <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Kahneman et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, affective heuristics are used as a replacement for risk-benefits assessments, especially under time pressure (Finucane et al., 2000; Slovic et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Additionally, affective heuristics are used as a replacement for risk-benefits assessments, especially under time pressure <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Finucane et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b188">Slovic et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, individual circumstances and prior experiences can shape the perception of risks and benefits.
A technology may appear particularly attractive when alternatives are limited or unattractive (M. K. Lee & Rich, 2021).
text.formatted: A technology may appear particularly attractive when alternatives are limited or unattractive (M. K. <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Lee & Rich, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For example, individuals without access to healthcare might value the benefits of AIgenerated medical advice more highly than the risk of receiving imperfect AI health advice or data (Schlicker, Lechner, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, individuals without access to healthcare might value the benefits of AIgenerated medical advice more highly than the risk of receiving imperfect AI health advice or data <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">(Schlicker, Lechner, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If an inaccurate risk-benefit assessment causes suboptimal performance, education and training of the user as well as proper communication of risk and uncertainty in system design can be effective countermeasures.
User training should address common fallacies in risk-assessment.

If risks are underestimated, it could, for instance, involve exposure to base rates and historical automation accidents and errors to give users a better idea about the probabilities and costs of the consequences (Bahner et al., 2008).

text.text: On the communication side Bostrom et al. (2023) denote: "Risk communication research […] shows [...] that the effects of visualizations and other communications of uncertainty on trust are likely to depend on the quality and context of communication [...].
Thus, there is a need for meaningful and useful information rather than just more information."
Simple changes in risk framing can influence human behavior, even if the odds are transparent (Kahneman & Tversky, 1984).
text.formatted: Simple changes in risk framing can influence human behavior, even if the odds are transparent <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Kahneman & Tversky, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Calibration Point 5 refers to relatively stable dispositions that moderate the relationship of trust related concepts, including the transitions from perceived trustworthiness to trust and from trust to trusting behavior (Figure 1).

text.text: This refers to concepts such as trust propensity (Mayer et al., 1995; Scholz et al., 2024), dispositional trust (Hoff & Bashir, 2015; Merritt & Ilgen, 2008), automation expectancy (Pop et al., 2015), risk propensity (Ferronato & Bashir, 2020; Mayer et al., 1995), as well as related concepts like the perfect automation schema (Lyons & Guznov, 2019; Matthews et al., 2020; Merritt, Unnerstall, et al., 2015), and (automation-induced) complacency potential (Merritt et al., 2019; Singh et al., 1993).

text.text: Given an accurate trustworthiness assessment, trust propensity influences a) how much evidence for the presence of trustworthiness a trustor needs (as reflected in the item of the Propensity to Trust in Automated Technology Scale [PTT-A]; Scholz et al., 2024: "Even though I may sometimes suffer the consequences of trusting automated technological systems, I still prefer to trust than not to trust them."), b) how much evidence for the absence of trustworthiness they tolerate (PTT-A item: "I believe that I am generally better off when I do not trust automated technological systems than when I trust them."), and c) how much uncertainty they tolerate (PTT-A item "I rarely trust automated technological systems because I can't handle the uncertainty.") to consider trusting.

text.text: All of this affects the likelihood of engaging in later steps of the trust development process, like considering the risks and benefits of using a system in a specific situation, and also to use or rely on it (i.e., to show trusting behavior).
What can be calibrated here is the range of uncertainty and vulnerability that should optimally be tolerated.
The extremes might vary from no evidence needed to trust (naïve mindset) to excessive evidence needed to trust (skeptical mindset).

Dispositional miscalibration is present if people hold extreme attitudes, i.e., they have strong aversion against or appreciation for systems in general or against a specific system (Dietvorst et al., 2015; Logg et al., 2019).

text.text: This may lead people to tolerate much uncertainty and evidence for the absence of trustworthiness, and still trust and rely on the system.

For instance, this case is reflected in an interpersonal trust-game context where Dunning et al. (2014) found across four studies that about 62% of their participants showed interpersonal trusting behavior, but only 20% of the participants considered their partner to be trustworthy.

text.text: Conversely, it could also happen that people have substantial evidence for the presence of trustworthiness, but still, they do not consider to trust or use a system that may benefit them (Dietvorst et al., 2015; Longoni et al., 2019).

text.text: Defining what degree of trust propensity is advantageous or disadvantageous for optimal joint performance brings up questions like: how much evidence is enough to rightfully trust a system?

Even if we cannot provide a satisfying answer to this question, we can conclude that it is beneficial to the joint human-system performance to avoid the extremes, i.e. having trustors who either always or never trust a system, who need excessive or very little evidence of trustworthiness, or who are willing to take any or no risk.
In these extreme cases we lose the potential of finding emergent capabilities of humans and systems working together.
To frame it differently, a trustor is "calibrated" at this point when they are open to incorporate new cues into their trustworthiness assessment.

For example, people with high expectations may develop more accurate trustworthiness assessments when understanding why automation errors occur (Dzindolet et al., 2003; Pop et al., 2015; Walliser et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, people with high expectations may develop more accurate trustworthiness assessments when understanding why automation errors occur <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Dzindolet et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">Pop et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b202">Walliser et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: If an extreme disposition or attitude leads to suboptimal joint human-system performance, effective countermeasures should focus on training and guiding trustors to stay aware of and potentially counter their own biases.

One approach is to enhance users' metacognitive awareness of their own biases, helping them recognize situations in which they are particularly susceptible to over-trusting or under-trusting the system (He et al., 2023).

text.text: Training interventions could incorporate scenario-based learning, real-time feedback, and reflection exercises to reinforce awareness of trust dynamics and their implications for performance (He et al., 2023).

text.text: Beyond individual training, it is crucial to develop effective methodologies to assess trust propensity and its stability over time.
This requires a deeper understanding of the factors that moderate trust dispositions, such as individual differences in cognitive styles, domain expertise, or exposure to technology.
It might be worthwhile to investigate certain categories of technologies that inherently elicit stronger trust or skepticism (e.g., in the medical domain, Longoni et al., 2019).

text.text: Additionally, ways to mitigate general tendencies to reject (AI) technologies may involve social proof mechanisms like user testimonials or expert reviews (Knowles & Richards, 2021; Scharowski et al., 2023), or individually tailored system solutions to counteract persistent presumptions (Costello et al., 2024; Okamura & Yamada, 2020).

text.text: Calibration Point 6 adopts a behavioral perspective and focuses exclusively on the calibration of observable trusting behavior, such as monitoring behavior or reliance on system advice or alerts.
Users are behaviorally calibrated when their actions match a predefined ideal behavior.
Once such an ideal behavioral pattern is specified, calibration can be assessed independently of the actual task outcome (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010).

text.text: Nevertheless, the desired outcome implicitly shapes what counts as ideal behavior (Figure 6).

text.text: Calibration Point 6 Note.
Calibration Point 6 refers to the calibration of the trustor's behavior to a defined ideal behavior.
The defined ideal behavior hence influences the outcome indirectly, and the outcome may inform the definition of an ideal behavior.
Behavioral adaptation does not necessarily require a deep understanding of the underlying system.
Instead, it relies on user compliance with prescribed behavioral rules.

The primary challenge at this calibration point lies in defining such rules that determine how much one should ideally monitor automation and how to appropriately rely and comply with it (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010; Parasuraman & Riley, 1997; Parasuraman & Wickens, 2008).

text.text: Determining what constitutes ideal behavior becomes particularly difficult when systems demand improvements in both accuracy and speed simultaneously, or when at least one dimension must be maintained while the other improves (Bahner et al., 2008).

text.text: Behavioral miscalibration occurs when users deviate from predefined ideal behavior.

Two well-studied manifestations of such miscalibration are automation complacency and automation bias, which are both considered behavioral manifestations of excessive trust in and reliance on automation (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010).

Similarly, trust has been directly conceptualized as monitoring intention (Loi et al., 2023), where higher trust was associated with reduced monitoring behavior (Patton & Wickens, 2024).

It was defined as "the tendency to use automated cues as a heuristic replacement for vigilant information seeking and processing" (Mosier & Skitka, 1996, p. 205).

text.text: Calibrating behavior at this point requires defining an ideal behavior.

For instance, for monitoring tasks ideal behavior may be optimal sampling behavior (i.e., how often a system should be monitored) based on the expected signal frequency (i.e., the Nyquist rate; Moray, 2003; Moray & Inagaki, 2000; Parasuraman et al., 2008).

text.text: In practice, defining ideal behavior can be difficult (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010), especially when working with self-learning AI systems whose internal processes are opaque and whose errors may occur unpredictably.

text.text: When ideal behavior can be defined, training can improve behavioral calibration.

For instance, exposing users to automation errors during training can foster more appropriate behavioral strategies, enhance multitasking performance, and reduce the impact of automation complacency (Bahner et al., 2008; Metzger et al., 2000; Walliser et al., 2023).

text.text: Note, once an ideal behavioral pattern is specified, it also becomes necessary to determine who is accountable when users behave in accordance with this ideal behavior, yet errors occur.
This issue becomes particularly salient in high-stakes domains like medicine where users are ultimately responsible for an outcome (European Data Protection Supervisor, 2025; Sterz et al., 2024).

Accordingly, it is important to clarify the accountabilities and responsibilities of different involved stakeholders (Mosier et al., 1997; Skitka et al., 2000).

text.text: Behavioral calibration depends on the existence of a normative behavioral standard.

When such standards cannot be established (e.g., when interacting with systems whose behavior is unpredictable, including large language models used for task support), interventions should shift toward earlier calibration points (CP1-CP5) that target system transparency or trustworthiness assessment rather than prescribing specific behavior.
Overall, there seems to be agreement on the goal of trust calibration to achieve optimal joint human-system performance.

However, there is conceptual and terminological heterogeneity on how this goal should be achieved and which role trust-related concepts play in this endeavor (Benk et al., 2024; Mehrotra et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, there is conceptual and terminological heterogeneity on how this goal should be achieved and which role trust-related concepts play in this endeavor <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Benk et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Mehrotra et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it is difficult to navigate the research field including its various terminology and operationalizations and to understand what and how to calibrate in order to optimize joint human-system performance.

Within the Trust Calibration-Points Framework (TCa-P) we integrate different approaches of trust calibration and consider trust calibration an umbrella term that reflects six distinct calibration points along the trust development process (Mayer et al., 1995; Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Within the Trust Calibration-Points Framework (TCa-P) we integrate different approaches of trust calibration and consider trust calibration an umbrella term that reflects six distinct calibration points along the trust development process <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Mayer et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We argue that each of these points can and need to be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance.
The TCa-P highlights what trust-related constructs can be calibrated, and provides a basis for how to calibrate these aspects.

The TCa-P advances the field by grounding calibration in a trust-process model, by improving terminological and conceptual clarity, and by providing a diagnostic tool for a long-standing challenge in human factors research and application: Identifying where miscalibration occurs in human-system interaction and countering it by the respective means.

In the following, we will elaborate on the theoretical and practical implications of the TCa-P on a broader level, and discuss limitations of the current approach as well as directions for future work.
One key question motivating this paper was: What is calibrated trust?
Our answer is that calibrated trust is a deceptively intuitive term that lacks precision.

The term "calibrated trust" disguises the actual goal of this research, as it suggests that the objective is to calibrate trust itself (J. D. Lee & See, 2004; Muir, 1987), whereas the actual underlying goal is optimal joint human-system performance (by means of trust-related factors).

D. <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Lee & See, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Muir, 1987)</ref>, whereas the actual underlying goal is optimal joint human-system performance (by means of trust-related factors).

text.text: Our analysis of prior work showed that the problem with prior monolithic perspectives on calibrated trust was that they lacked at least one of the aspects necessary for calibration: a clear goal and a tolerance range (answering the question: Towards what should be calibrated?), relevant influencing factors (What can be calibrated?), and means to influence these factors (How can these factors be adjusted?).
We want to stress here that the TCa-P is not just an integration of prior work, but also an invitation to shift the perspective on how we think about trust calibration in general.

To clarify the holistic perspective on trust calibration as proposed in the TCa-P, let us think through calibration in another context: the case of boiling a perfect egg for breakfast (Chakraborty et al., 2025; Figure 7).
text.formatted: To clarify the holistic perspective on trust calibration as proposed in the TCa-P, let us think through calibration in another context: the case of boiling a perfect egg for breakfast <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Chakraborty et al., 2025</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">7</ref>).

text.text: First, the goal must be defined, e.g., a soft-boiled vs.
hard-boiled egg.
Alongside the goal, a tolerance range must be specified, i.e., what is considered an acceptable egg, because not every deviation from the optimum necessarily constitutes failure.
Second, the relevant influencing factors must be identified, such as egg size and type, temperature, and altitude (cf. Chakraborty et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Second, the relevant influencing factors must be identified, such as egg size and type, temperature, and altitude (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Chakraborty et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Third, one must determine how to actually influence these egg-related factors, e.g., by changing the heat or the time in the water, by chosing smaller or larger eggs, or by climbing a hill.
To which degree one influencing factor needs to be adapted depends on the other factors, e.g., how long the egg should remain in the water depends on the temperature and the altitude.

In any case the resulting configuration should reflect for each influencing factor an ideal value ("the ought") to which the current value ("the is") should be adjusted in order to achieve the set goal, e.g., if the current temperature is 30° it needs to be adjusted to reach the ought-value of 100°.
This example should illustrate a more general principle of calibration.
Calibration is most likely not a one-shot adjustment of a single variable, but a process in which multiple interacting factors are adjusted towards a defined goal.

In this sense, the described process is closely connected to kibernetic systems, in which each factor can influence the others, and in which the calibration of one factor alone may not suffice to reach a specific goal (Carver & Scheier, 2000; Gaube et al., 2026; Schrills, 2025).

To meaningfully move forward with "trust calibration", we suggest using the term as an umbrella for the process of calibrating trust-related factors to achieve whatever is considered optimal performance.

The TCa-P offers a framework that enables specificity in determining a goal, the influencing factors to achieve this goal, and a structure to determine how these factors can be meaningfully influenced towards this goal.
Additionally, the TCa-P offers a more precise terminology supporting this specification.

Instead of referring to general terms like calibrated trust (and the often-used but vague associated terms of over-or undertrust), we suggest to refer clearly to a specific calibration point, i.e., expectations regarding the optimal joint human-system performance (CP1), the degree of accuracy (respectively justification) of trustworthiness assessments (CP2), the (mis)alignment between users, systems and normative standards (CP3), the degree of accuracy of risk-benefit assessments (CP4), variations of trust dispositions (CP5), and the degree of adaptation to a behavioral ideal (CP6), or a combination of those (see Table 1).

text.text: Beyond providing a conceptual framework for understanding trust calibration and the practical implications outlined at each calibration point, the TCa-P framework can also support practical challenges in the design and governance of human-AI interaction.
One example is effective human oversight, which has become a central requirement for the deployment of AI in high-risk domains (European Data Protection Supervisor, 2025).

Effective human oversight provides a useful example of the practical relevance of the TCa-P because many of the challenges associated with effective oversight are, at their core, challenges of trust calibration.

For example, Article 14 of the European AI Act requires that human operators understand the capabilities and limitations of AI systems, appropriately monitor and interpret their outputs, remain aware of their potential (automation) bias, decide when to rely on or override AI recommendations, and intervene when necessary (European Data Protection Supervisor, 2025).

Similar to issues around calibrated trust as outlined in the beginning of this paper, it is currently not clear how effective human oversight should be achieved and evaluated, i.e., what the standards are to consider oversight effective (or at least acceptable) (Sterz et al., 2024; van Voorst, 2024).

text.text: The TCa-P provides a structured framework for identifying the normative questions that need to be answered to achieve an appropriate reference standard that could help in determining when human oversight is considered effective.
More specifically, the TCa-P can guide this process, by supporting to ask the right questions when defining an ideal reference or calibration standard (Figure 8).

text.text: Not only "what should be calibrated?", and "how should be calibrated?"
are important questions, but also "towards what should be calibrated?"
"Towards what?"
refers to normative questions that need to be discussed when implementing AI systems into high-risk contexts.
For example, Calibration Point 1 requires defining the goal of human oversight, i.e., when oversight can be considered fulfilled.
Calibration Points 2-4 require specifying what counts as accurate and justified trustworthiness and risk-benefit assessments and to which standards users and systems should be aligned.
Calibration Point 5 requires defining unacceptable dispositions.
Calibration Point 6 requires specifying the behavioral standards that users are expected to follow in each context (e.g., monitoring strategies that define adequate human oversight).

Together, these normative reference standards establish a calibration blueprint that enables systematic comparison between the desired ("ought") and the observed ("is") state of factors influencing human-AI interaction (Figure 8) (Schlicker, 2026).

The "ought" question specifies the ideal reference potentially including a tolerance range, and the "is/are" questions specify the status quo.

Such reference standards may also provide a basis for questions and discussions of accountability.
If users comply with predefined calibration standards, occurring errors may rather indicate limitations of the AI system than failures of human oversight.

For example, if users are instructed to verify AI recommendations only below a predefined confidence threshold expressed by the AI system, errors occurring despite compliance with this behavioral standard may point to miscalibrated confidence estimates within the system rather than inadequate human oversight (Hunsicker et al., 2026).

Trust calibration is a complex and dynamic process, and future research may reveal further nuances that refine or expand the model.

For example, signal detection theory has been proposed as a different perspective on trust calibration (Langer et al., 2024; Sheridan, 2019), while other trust models emphasize learned, temporal, specificity or delegation components that may introduce additional calibration mechanisms (Castelfranchi & Falcone, 2010; Hoff & Bashir, 2015; J. text.text: A second limitation concerns the empirical operationalization of the framework.

While the TCa-P is theoretically grounded, it remains an open question to what extent individual calibration points can be measured distinctively and reliably (Kohn et al., 2021; Tenhundfeld et al., 2022).

text.text: Several calibration points require normative reference standards that may be difficult to define in practice.

For instance, defining maximum joint performance in complex tasks, determining what counts as accurate or justified trustworthiness assessment of non-deterministic AI systems, or defining ideal behavioral adaptation may not always be straightforward.

Nevertheless, we believe that a proper understanding and definition of the problem and potential solutions on a conceptual level are a necessary requirement for the similarly grand challenge of developing methods to achieve these solutions.

If we do not specify the expectation regarding the outcome we might achieve the goal without noticing, and potentially call it inappropriate reliance (implicitly blaming a user who might have justifiably followed system advice [CP2], or has legitimately different individual standards [CP3]).

text.text: While the TCa-P adds complexity to the issue of calibrating trust-related phenomena to optimize the joint human-system performance, we advocate to embrace this complexity rather than to oversimplify the concept up to the degree that it is neither diagnostic nor useful.

A valuable step for future research might be to define normative reference standards against which calibration can be validated, and to develop ways to operationalize the validation of calibration points, and means to adequately influence these points towards a defined standard.
Building on this work, future research could develop targeted methods to diagnose miscalibrations at each point.

For example, interdependency analysis, which assesses the relative strengths of humans and machines within a team, may be particularly suited for Calibration Point 1 (Centeio Jorge et al., 2024; M. Johnson et al., 2014; M. Johnson & Bradshaw, 2021), whereas human error identification methods that aim to categorize human errors (e.g., detection vs. utilization errors) may be suitable for Calibration Points 2 and 4 (Cheng & Hwang, 2015; Kirwan & Ainsworth, 1992; Stanton, 2017).

text.text: Such work could establish a methodological toolbox that links diagnostic methods to specific calibration points across various application contexts.

Conclusion "Trust calibration" was defined and operationalized heterogeneously, often focusing on separate aspects of the trust development process while sharing the common goal of optimizing joint human-system performance.

The Trust Calibration-Points Framework (TCa-P) integrates these different approaches by conceptualizing trust calibration as a process comprising six calibration points that can be calibrated to achieve optimal joint humansystem performance.
Thereby, the TCa-P advances conceptual and terminological clarity, and enables a more holistic and diagnostic understanding of trust calibration.

Rather than asking whether "trust is calibrated", researchers and practitioners can identify which component of the trust development process is not where it ought to be and select interventions that specifically target this factor.

This perspective supports more targeted research, more specific system design and user training, and may also provide a structured framework for evaluating the effectiveness of human-system interaction, which can be especially valuable for highstakes applications of AI requiring human oversight.
Furthermore, our perspective on trust calibration may inspire novel ways for research and practice, and can support the safe integration of AI systems into human decision-making.
